| | |
|---|---|
| **Format** | Team project (2–3 students), written design document + oral defense |
| **Weight** | 20 % of the final grade |

## Context

Kyiv School of Economics is integrating artificial intelligence into its educational process: LLM-based tutors, automated feedback on assignments, tools that help faculty prepare course materials, and new assessment formats. Every such initiative is, at its core, a hypothesis — *"this tool will improve learning."* A hypothesis without measurement is a belief, not knowledge.

Your task is to design an experiment that would allow the university to test whether a specific application of AI genuinely improves educational outcomes — without causing harm along the way.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Why This Matters

The strongest projects will be considered as blueprints for real pilots at KSE. This is not a classroom fiction: your design decisions may shape how the university deploys AI.
:::

## Your Task

AI adoption in a university happens at different **levels**, and each level opens a distinct hypothesis space with its own measurement challenges. Choose **one level and one direction**, then develop a complete experimental design. You may propose your own direction, subject to instructor approval.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Student Level

The tool is used by students; the effect is measured on students. Hundreds of observation units are typically available.

1. **AI tutor for a specific course** — a chat assistant answering student questions based on course materials.
2. **AI note-taking assistant** — automatic lecture summaries and condensed study notes.
3. **Adaptive practice problems** — AI generates individualized exercises matched to each student's level.

### Faculty Level

The tool is used by instructors; the effect is measured both on faculty (workload, material quality) and, indirectly, on students. Only dozens of observation units are available.

4. **Automated rubric-based feedback** — AI evaluates assignment drafts against the instructor's rubric and returns comments before the deadline.
5. **AI-assisted course preparation** — a tool for creating materials, exercises, and quizzes; measured via preparation time and course quality.
6. **AI-resilient assessment redesign** — the instructor switches to an assignment format robust to dishonest AI use.

### Administrative Level

Decisions are made by academic directors, deans, or university leadership; the effect is measured at the level of programs. Only a handful of units exist.

7. **Early detection of at-risk students** — AI analytics over LMS activity alerts the academic director to students who need support.
8. **AI-use policy comparison** — different policy formats (prohibition / regulated use / free use with disclosure) compared across programs or courses.
9. **AI-assisted curriculum review** — a tool for analyzing syllabi and program coherence.

:::

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## The Level Determines the Statistics

The level of implementation dictates your randomization unit and your realistic sample size: **hundreds** of students, **dozens** of instructors, or a **handful** of programs. These are fundamentally different statistical problems, and your design must reflect that honestly.
:::

## Design Checklist (Roadmap)

Work through every item below. Each item is a mandatory section of your document.

A companion **[experiment design checklist](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1oRnvwWaC7iFjA3qBNHXmB3drmL_-JXM0/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=114058542940348489102&rtpof=true&sd=true)** accompanies this assignment. Make a copy for your team and keep it updated as you work: every item must end up as ✓, as ✗ with a comment, or as *n/a* with a justification — an empty cell is not a state. The first sheet covers the design phase (your project scope); the second shows what a real pilot goes through after the design is approved — reference it in your Decision Plan (@sec-actionplan). Each checklist item points to the corresponding section of this document.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Depth Priorities for a Two-Week Timeline

Maximum depth is expected in @sec-hypothesis (hypothesis), @sec-randomization (randomization unit), @sec-metrics (metrics), @sec-power through @sec-variance (the statistical core with simulations), and @sec-validity (threats to validity). Sections @sec-problem, @sec-feasibility, @sec-segment, @sec-arms, and @sec-actionplan may be brief — one or two paragraphs each. Target length: **4–6 pages** excluding code — prefer tables and the checklist structure over long prose. A narrow design carried through to the end beats a broad, shallow one.
:::

### Problem Statement {#sec-problem}

What problem are you solving? Why does it matter to the university? What evidence suggests the problem exists (data, observations, complaints)?

### Hypothesis {#sec-hypothesis}

Start with the basic structure to get the causal logic right:

> **If** we [deploy such-and-such intervention in such-and-such way],
> **then** it will [affect a specified segment], leading to [a change in a specified metric by a specified amount],
> **because** [arguments about the mechanism of impact on the learning process].

Then upgrade it to the **quantified form** required in your document — a single statement that already contains the numbers your statistical sections will use:

> We believe that **[intervention]**, for **[segment]**, will **[increase / decrease]** **[primary metric]** from a baseline of **[X]** to at least **[Y]**, based on **[evidence or mechanism]**. We will measure this over **[timeframe]**, with an MDE of **[Z]**, while monitoring **[guardrail metrics]** to ensure no harm.

This form is deliberately hard to fill in: you cannot complete it without knowing your baseline, committing to an MDE, and naming your guardrails. If a blank refuses to be filled, that is the design telling you what you have not thought through yet — not a formatting inconvenience.

Two hard requirements:

- The hypothesis must be **falsifiable**: it should be clear in advance which outcome would refute it.
- The hypothesis must be **fixed before any outcome data are seen**. Inventing or adjusting the hypothesis after looking at results is post hoc theorizing (HARKing): the explanation is fitted to the data, nothing can refute it, and the "finding" cannot be trusted. Your pre-registered hypothesis is the one you defend — including when the data disagree with it.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Not Every Comparison Is an Experiment

Comparing two options without a hypothesis is not an experiment — it may be *exploration* (observing to generate ideas), *hedging* (shipping several variants because you are unsure), or simply pitting variants against each other without caring why one wins. Exploration is a legitimate and useful activity — but it produces hypotheses, not conclusions. If your team cannot state a falsifiable hypothesis yet, say so honestly and design an exploratory study first; do not dress it up as an experiment.
:::

### Feasibility {#sec-feasibility}

What does deployment cost (licenses, faculty time, technical support)? What change in the metric would justify this cost? Are there simpler alternatives worth testing first?

### Randomization Unit {#sec-randomization}

This is the pivotal design decision — and in education it is far harder than in product analytics. Choose and justify:

| Unit | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| **Student** | Maximum statistical power | High interference risk: students talk, share tools and notes |
| **Section / study group** | Reduced interference | Cluster randomization: effective sample size shrinks — account for intraclass correlation (ICC) and the design effect |
| **Course / cohort** | Near-zero interference | Critically few units; comparability of courses is questionable |
| **Instructor** | Natural unit for faculty-level interventions | Only dozens of units; instructor effects dominate the variance |
| **Program / faculty** | Matches administrative-level decisions | So few units that classical randomization may be impossible |

The randomization unit must match the level of implementation: if the *instructor* receives the tool, randomizing students within that instructor's course is usually meaningless — the effect reaches all of them at once.

For the administrative level, where only a few programs exist, it is acceptable — and expected — to justify a **quasi-experimental design**: stepped-wedge rollout, historical-cohort comparison with covariate adjustment, or difference-in-differences. In that case, state explicitly which assumptions substitute for randomization and how plausible they are.

Your section must describe: the assignment mechanism (or its quasi-experimental substitute), the balance check across arms (prior performance, year of study, major), and your assessment of interference risk between arms.

### Experiment Segment {#sec-segment}

Who participates: which course, year, faculty? New students or everyone? Inclusion and exclusion criteria? How many students are realistically available per semester — and what does that imply for the experiment's duration?

### Experiment Arms {#sec-arms}

Describe the control and treatment arms precisely enough for another researcher to reproduce them. What exactly does a student (or instructor) see and do in each arm? What counts as "using" the tool (event, frequency, duration)? How do you prevent the control group from adopting the same tool on its own?

### Metrics {#sec-metrics}

Complete the table for each metric type:

| Metric | Baseline | MDE (abs) | Sample size & duration | Test / method | Comment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary** | | | | | |
| **Informational** | | | | | |
| **Guardrail** | | | | | |
| **Proxy** | | | | | |

Education-specific guidance:

- **Primary metric** — a learning outcome: final assessment score, gain between pre-test and post-test, share of students reaching a threshold level. Justify why this metric captures *learning* rather than mere activity.
- **Informational metrics** — engagement, frequency of tool use, time on task, satisfaction.
- **Guardrail metrics** — what must *not* deteriorate: academic-integrity indicators, equity of outcomes between stronger and weaker students (does the tool widen the gap?), ability to solve problems *without* the tool, faculty workload, student well-being.
- **Proxy metrics** — fast signals correlated with the primary metric: midterm results, draft quality.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## The Central Measurement Trap

How will you distinguish *"the student learned"* from *"the student submitted work the AI produced"*? Address this explicitly — it is the single most common failure mode of AI-in-education experiments.
:::

### Sample Size and Power {#sec-power}

Hyperparameters: $\alpha = 0.05$, power $= 0.8$ (justify any deviation).

Compute the required sample size for the primary metric at your chosen MDE. Compare it with the number of students actually available. If you fall short — the typical situation in education — state what you sacrifice: a larger MDE, a longer experiment spanning several cohorts, a one-sided test, or variance reduction.

Under cluster randomization, the calculation **must** incorporate the design effect.

For faculty- and administrative-level designs, sample sizes are orders of magnitude smaller than in student-level experiments. Asymptotic properties will not save you here: consider exact tests, permutation tests, and nonparametric methods, and show honestly in simulation which MDE you can detect at all with the units available. The conclusion *"with 8 instructors we can reliably detect only a very large effect, so we propose a two-year, multi-cohort design"* is a strong result — not a weakness of the project.

### Choice and Validation of the Statistical Test {#sec-test}

Justify the test for your primary metric. Educational data are rarely normal: scores are bounded by the scale, distributions are skewed, and group variances may differ. Consider both parametric options (Welch's *t*-test) and nonparametric alternatives (Mann–Whitney *U*, Brunner–Munzel), and explain precisely which hypothesis each of them tests.

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## Simulation-Based Validation — Mandatory

Generate synthetic data that plausibly mimic your metrics (distribution shape, sample size) and run:

- **1,000 A/A simulations:** the false-positive rate must be $\approx \alpha$, and the p-value distribution must be uniform;
- **1,000 A/B simulations** with an injected effect equal to your MDE: the detection rate must match the declared power.

The simulation code (R or Python) with a **fixed random seed** is submitted with the project and must reproduce end-to-end.
:::

### Variance Reduction {#sec-variance}

Will you use students' prior performance (GPA, entry test) as a covariate (CUPED)? Estimate in simulation how much this shrinks the required sample size under a plausible correlation between prior and final performance.

### Threats to Validity {#sec-validity}

Analyze at least the following:

- **Novelty effect** — initial enthusiasm for a new tool that fades over time.
- **Hawthorne effect** — participants behave differently because they know they are being observed.
- **Interference (spillover)** — the control group gains access to the tool or its outputs.
- **Differential attrition** — weaker (or stronger) students drop out of one arm more often.
- **Semester seasonality** — workload and motivation shift from the first week to the exam period.

For each threat: how does your design mitigate it, and how would you diagnose it after the fact?

### Ethics {#sec-ethics}

An educational experiment is an experiment on people — and its participants are students whose grades and learning carry real consequences. Describe:

- **Informed consent:** what participants are told, and how.
- **No-harm guarantee:** the experiment's outcome cannot lower any student's final grade.
- **Equal access:** if the tool proves useful, the control group receives it after the experiment ends.
- **Confidentiality** of performance data.

### Decision Plan {#sec-actionplan}

- **Success** (primary metric improved, guardrails intact): [what the university does next]
- **Failure** (primary metric declined, or a guardrail fired): [what you do]
- **Null result:** is this evidence of no effect? What about power? A second iteration?

## Deliverables and Defense

The defense takes place as a presentation before the class and invited experts:

- **Up to 7 minutes** — presentation of the design. Focus on *decisions*, not a walkthrough of the checklist: why this randomization unit, where the MDE comes from, what the simulation showed.
- **2–3 minutes** — questions. Every team member must be able to answer for **any** part of the project.

Submitted before the defense: the design document, your team's completed copy of the checklist, simulation code, and slides.

## Grading Rubric (100 points)

| Component | Points | What is assessed |
|---|---|---|
| Hypothesis & metrics | 20 | Falsifiability; the metric captures learning rather than activity; thoughtful guardrails |
| Randomization design | 20 | Justified unit choice; interference analysis; cluster corrections where needed |
| Statistical core | 25 | Correct sample-size calculation; justified test choice; working A/A and A/B simulation validation |
| Threats to validity & ethics | 15 | Depth of analysis; realistic mitigation mechanisms |
| Realism & feasibility | 10 | The experiment can actually be run at KSE with available resources |
| Defense | 10 | Clarity of presentation; quality of answers from every team member |

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Penalties

A simulation that does not reproduce with the fixed seed: **−10 points**. Missing guardrail metrics: **−10 points**.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why Day 7 Is Mandatory

The mid-point consultation exists so that no team spends the second week simulating a misdesigned experiment. Come with specific questions, not a blank page.
:::

## Practical Guidance

- The document structure is adapted from industry A/B-testing practice; the key differences in education are **small samples, clustered structure, interference, and ethical obligations** toward participants.
- Do not try to measure everything: one sharp experiment with one primary metric beats an ambitious plan that cannot be executed.
- A null result under insufficient power does **not** mean "AI doesn't work" — it means "we could not have seen it." Keep these conclusions apart.
